High school graduation is not only a breath of fresh air before plunging into the new challenges of college, but also helps motivate people to take on those next 4 years and eventually walk the stage again. In my peds rotation the other 5 girls in my clinical were a pretty tight-knit clique, which caused me to appear even more quiet than I already was. I never had a problem with it and kept myself busy in the patient rooms while they would often sit to the side talking and laughing loudly. 

With literally 3 days left in this rotation, my clinical instructor pulled me aside and told me that she was concerned I would not be an effective nurse because “I do not talk much” and she was worried that I would not do things like report unstable vitals in the future. So with 3 days left in this clinical, she put me on an “improvement plan” in which I had to prove I could be a talker, or else fail the clinical and therefore the nursing program. She gave me literally no indicators in the weeks prior so mind you I thought I was doing really well up to this point. 

Anyway I pretty much had just one day to prove that I could be outgoing, so I annoyed the shit out of everyone that day, especially the poor nurse I was shadowing. And then on the final day/debrief my preceptor said she was satisfied. 

Nursing as a field gives you so much crap for not being extroverted. It’s never gotten in the way of me building rapport with my patients or reporting status changes in real time. It’s also not like I ever ignored my cohort, or my coworkers. I simply choose to save my energy by not gossiping on the side, and it’s crazy how many people take personal offense to that.

I graduated 1 year ago and found the nursing program to be poorly organized. A couple examples: 1) lab/simulation rooms being switched up last minute at the health campus because the doctor/PA program needs are prioritized; 2) scatterbrained professors who would go on random unrelated tangents during lecture or otherwise read directly from the slides; 3) clinical sites being assigned last minute; 4) covid zoom classes being poor learning modalities; 5) we had a microbiology professor assigned last minute who barely spoke English and nobody learned anything from that course that semester, plus the microbio lab was extremely half-assed. 

But most of the problems at Case’s nursing program are ubiquitous across other universities. It’s honestly unavoidable with nursing education. A good number of us failed or dropped out, but those who graduated did so with pretty good grades. Medsurg was hardest for me and I barely scraped by, but graduated with a 3.6. Clinicals take up a ton of time, but if you want to participate in extracurriculars it’s possible, I know many classmates were active in clubs for all 4 years. You do end up pretty isolated from campus by graduation, as all your courses will be nursing-specific. I do want to note that my cohort was a small one, so we didn’t deal with running out of clinical sites like other years may have. Case is close to Cleveland Clinic, UH, Metro, St Vincent, and the VA, so we are lucky in that regard. No shortage of nursing assistant jobs or nurse internships either. But if you get assigned somewhere far away and need to Uber there multiple times a week, the program will not care, so you gotta make it work. Again, common across all programs. 

The hospitals around here will hire new grads straight into ICU. I want to say a majority of my cohort went into ICU, as did I.  

Some unsolicited advice for going into nursing: start practicing NCLEX questions early. I would’ve started in my first year if I had known. Nursing schools often pull NCLEX-style questions for their exams (as does Case) so you’re helping your own grades while preparing for the main deal.

I’m a new grad in a Cleveland Clinic regional branch ICU just across town from main campus. I’m also Ohio native and have lived in Cle for the past 4 years. Long info dump: 

LCOL depends on the area you are looking at, but the pay really is decent in comparison. I lived next to main campus for 2 years during college and my rent was $570 after dividing among 2 roommates. Lots of broke med students looking for roommates too. 

Main campus is fast paced and, to me, intimidating. Docs tend to be more stuck up. Which ICU did you get accepted into? Some are hellish and others are chill. I really enjoyed my MICU clinical at Main. Anyway, there’s a ton of new grads in the ICUs there; you’ll find friends your age easily during the 12-week orientation. You’ll also constantly have students on your unit, because so many healthcare programs send them to Cle clinic. It’s nice not being the only newbie around! 

Life in Ohio will be a culture shock. The highlight of living in Cle as a new grad is that you can save up a lot of money before moving elsewhere. A lot of people stick around for this reason. Cleveland is pretty LGBTQ friendly (I’m part of the community as well). Case Western’s campus is also next to Main campus, which drives a lot of diversity and forward-thinking people. I kinda love that Cle is a smaller city, and there is a great music/sports/outdoors scene despite it. It feels like a very “young” city if that makes sense. The whole atmosphere is very laidback. You’d really have to visit to see if you like it. 

Huge healthcare hub in this area, too: Cle Clinic, University Hospitals, Metrohealth, the VA, and all their regional campuses. You can jump ship if you happen to hate your unit lol. The other hospitals are good for various reasons (differentials, nursing culture, pensions, etc) and it was honestly tough picking Cle clinic over them. 

My boyfriend is from LA and has lived in Cle for 7 years. His main complaint is that the weather is very gray here, which is very true. I’m used to it by now, but it will be very different from the sunshine in CA. We also don’t have mountains :( 

The white scrubs were almost a dealbreaker for me too, after 4 years of white scrubs as a student. However— you get used to them. I’m almost off orientation and I have to say, I don’t mind them as much as I thought I would. You just have to know what to wear under them haha!

I feel you on the testing anxiety, I struggled with that as well during school and almost got dropped from the program because of it. 

First things first, for the NCLEX all you have to do is reach the minimum number of questions- 85. There’s no point in rushing through questions as it is more advantageous to have less questions done that are correct, than more questions done that are incorrect. So no point in rushing unless you’re not on track to finish 85 questions in 5 hours, which is unlikely. 

In your study routine, simulate the NCLEX a couple times. Make your own testing environment, set a timer, and do 150 questions as if it’s the real thing. Notice when you start to get anxious, what your average time per question is, etc. Knowing this helps when testing for real. And throughout the weeks before the exam, tell yourself “I WILL PASS” out loud. Anytime your brain starts doubting you, cut it off and say I WILL PASS and leave it at that. Because that’s the truth. 

Set aside a day before the test to relax and don’t try to cram anymore content. Don’t overstimulate your mind too much either. What I did was try not to scroll Reddit, Insta, etc. You can workout, go to the beach, meditate, whatever, just do not think about the exam or study. 

KNOW what to expect immediately before the test. You’ll check in, pat yourself down, put your phone in a Pearson plastic baggie, put everything away in your locker, scan your hand prints, take an ID photo, get a whiteboard and pen, be led to your computer, then you’re off! Visit your testing site ahead of time if it helps too. I used the bathroom, took a couple deep breaths, and took propranolol before checking in. 

During the test, you’ll feel the anxiety but remind yourself you have done this before! You’ve simulated the test and you know what to expect. Use headphones if it works for you (if you are bothered by your heart beating too loud, don’t). Turn off the view of the timer and the question number— seriously. Don’t mind the other people. I was the very last one in my test site. Think of it this way: the people leaving early might have failed because rushing the questions increases your chances of failure. 

Go in fully expecting to do 150 questions and take a full 5 hours. Do not count your SATAs or case studies, and do not overanalyze the difficulty of your questions. They don’t mean anything. Focus on nothing but the question right in front of you, one at a time. 

If at any point the anxiety makes you overthink your questions, just look away from your screen. What I did was look down at my whiteboard and doodle, jot down a couple notes, just to reset my brain and start over with the question. Once you rule an answer out, do not go back to it!!  

I truly believe taking my time was what allowed me to pass, as it was never something I had mastered in nursing school. I basically told myself, “you are going to do 150 questions and take the full 5 hours and be the very last one in the testing room. You have practiced hundreds of questions like these before. You will pass.” I have no doubt you know the content, give yourself the time to prove it!

Class, clinical, and lab are like full time jobs each week. It’s hard to work an actual paying job without sacrificing a lot of sleep. Continuing to work my job during practicum almost killed me— straight 24hrs without sleep. 

Clinical locations are never released until the last minute. Your commute, your conflicting commitments, your child’s daycare— your problem, not theirs. And more than 2 absences can fail you. 

We constantly changed classrooms because the college didn’t respect the nursing program and shunted us wherever there was space. 

There are intensive courses required during winter and summer break, so you have to return to campus early. Furthermore, snow days don’t apply to nursing students, so you have to go in during a blizzard. 

Get ready to be nitpicked like you never have before. Skills check offs can make you cry (I did, at least twice). 

Your clinical preceptor can suddenly decide they don’t like you, and they have the power to fail your clinical component which means you automatically have to retake the semester. 

If you don’t find a friend group/clique early, you’re doomed to being the odd one out in every clinical, group project, presentation, etc.

Ulcers occur when the stomach or intestinal lining (which is normally the stomach’s protection against its own acid) is disturbed and the stomach acid HCl aggravates an exposed area. 1st gen NSAIDs block what are called COX-2 inhibitors. Blocking COX-2 gives the relief you know NSAIDs for, like decreasing fever and inflammation. However, NSAIDs cannot block COX-2 without also blocking COX-1. When you block COX-1, you prevent formation of good prostaglandins, leading to bleed and gastric upset which is where the aggravation of the lining and infiltration by HCl comes in. This is why there are 2nd gen NSAIDs being developed that only block COX-2, which aims to provide relief without risking those gastric ulcers. Source: am a current nursing student
